960.title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
960.hook: Martin Luther King Jr, jailed, writes to fellow clergy that injustice in one place threatens justice in every place
960.howItsDone: Some Christians read King's letter in churches, classrooms and study groups, and some congregations read parts of it aloud together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Billy Graham, an old hymn, and ropes coming down. Your line: just as I am.

A cell in the Birmingham city jail. A pastor has been arrested for leading a march in defiance of a court order. A newspaper reaches him, with a public statement from a group of white clergymen in the city. They call the demonstrations unwise and untimely. They say outsiders are stirring up trouble, and the right course is patience and the courts. The pastor has no desk and not much paper. The story goes that he starts his answer in the margins of that very newspaper, and on scraps smuggled in and out. The pastor is Martin Luther King Jr., writing to fellow ministers.

The letter is full of the Bible and the church. To the charge that he was an outsider, he answered that he was in Birmingham because injustice was there, and compared himself to the apostle Paul, who left his home town to carry the gospel to other cities. Then a claim readers still quote: injustice in one place is a threat to justice in every place. In his picture, all people are bound together in a single garment of destiny, so a tear in one part runs through the whole cloth. To the charge that the time wasn't right, he wrote that for Black Americans the word wait had nearly always meant never. On breaking laws, he reached back to Augustine and Thomas Aquinas, saints of the church, to argue that an unjust law is no true law at all, while insisting that anyone who breaks one must do it openly, lovingly, and accept the penalty. He reached for the prophet Amos too. In the King James Bible: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." Not a trickle, saved for a better season. A river. Some of the letter's sharpest words aren't aimed at open enemies, but at the white moderate, who agrees with the goal in principle and keeps asking for patience, and at white churches that stood by. King wrote with grief about the church, not against it. He was a pastor, disappointed in his own house, and he still called it home.

Think of one unfairness close to you that isn't happening to you: a coworker always talked over, a neighbor without a ramp, a school rule that lands harder on some kids. Look at it plainly, notice the part of you that says it's not the right time, and find one small, honest word you could say. If you pray, hold Amos's line about justice running down like water.
Birmingham, where Martin Luther King Jr. wrote from a cell to fellow clergy who had told him to wait.
Your line: justice is all one piece. One garment of destiny. Nine hundred sixty days now.

961.title: The mountaintop
961.hook: the night before he is killed, King says he's seen the promised land
961.howItsDone: Some churches in the United States remember King's life and words near his birthday, and the mountaintop speech is sometimes played or read aloud at those services.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Birmingham, a letter written in the margins. Your line: justice is all one piece.

Rain and wind outside a church in Memphis. Sanitation workers in the city are on strike, carrying signs that say they are men, and Martin Luther King Jr. has come to stand with them. He's tired, with a sore throat. He nearly stays at the hotel, but the people waiting call him, and he comes. He speaks a long time: the strike, the Good Samaritan, the road ahead. Near the end, he talks about his own life, and how long it might be. The next evening, he is shot and killed on a motel balcony.

In the closing minutes, King said he had been to the mountaintop. He had looked over and seen the promised land. He might not get there with them, he said, but they, as a people, would get there. And he wasn't worried; he feared no one. Listeners who knew their Bibles would have heard where that came from. At the end of Deuteronomy, Moses has led his people out of slavery and through the wilderness. He climbs to the top of Pisgah, and God shows him the whole land spread out below. Then God says, in the King James Bible: "I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither." Moses sees it, but doesn't enter. He dies there, and the people go on without him. King placed himself in that story, and it isn't a hopeless one. The letter to the Hebrews describes the old heroes of faith the same way: "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them." Seeing from far off is still seeing. Hope, in this picture, doesn't depend on getting there yourself. King ended that night with the opening line of the Battle Hymn of the Republic: "Mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord." Then he stepped back from the pulpit. Some listeners remember the speech for its strange calm: a man who sounds as if he senses what may be coming, and has made his peace with not crossing over.

962.title: Fannie Lou Hamer
962.hook: a sharecropper beaten for registering voters sings This Little Light of Mine
962.howItsDone: Black churches in the United States sing This Little Light of Mine in worship, and it was sung at mass meetings and marches of the civil rights movement.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mountaintop, and Moses seeing a land he wouldn't enter. Your line: look toward the promised land.

A bus full of tired people is rolling back from a county courthouse in Mississippi. They've just tried to register to vote, and been turned away. Police stop the bus on a made-up charge. Fear goes through the seats like a draft. Then one woman, a sharecropper who spent long years in the cotton fields, starts to sing. A church song. Others join in. That woman is Fannie Lou Hamer. That evening the plantation owner tells her to take back her registration or leave. She leaves.

Hamer grew up in the Mississippi Delta, in a family of sharecroppers, and she grew up in church. When young organizers came asking Black citizens to register to vote, she raised her hand. It cost her the home and the work she had, and later more. Coming back from a voter workshop, she and others were arrested in the town of Winona, and in that jail she was beaten so badly she carried the injuries for life. She didn't stop. She sang. Her song was This Little Light of Mine, a gospel song sung in Black churches, and she sang it on buses, in mass meetings, outside courthouses, and, people remember, in jail. It echoes Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount. In the King James Bible: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid." And: "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house." A bushel was a basket for measuring grain. Nobody lights a lamp and puts a basket over it. Hamer's little light wasn't small in the end. She told her story to a committee of a national political convention, on television, and asked out loud whether this was the country it claimed to be. She's remembered for saying she was tired of being tired. She also spoke plainly of loving the people who hurt her, because her faith asked it. A small light, in her life, meant one voice that would not go back under the basket.

Hum This Little Light of Mine, or any song about light, or sing one line under your breath; if singing isn't for you, light a candle or a lamp and watch it a while. Notice how a small flame fills a dark room, and think of one good thing you've kept under a basket. If you pray, hold Jesus's words: ye are the light of the world.

Your line: this little light. Out from under the basket, and giving light. Until tomorrow.

963.title: Vatican II (1962–65)
963.hook: the Catholic Church opens its windows: Mass in local languages, new respect for other churches
963.howItsDone: Catholic parishes today celebrate Mass in local languages, with readings from both Testaments, while some parishes also celebrate the older Latin form.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Winona, and a woman singing on a stopped bus. Your line: this little light.

A small book with a ribbon in it, worn soft at the corners. It's an old Catholic missal, and on each page the prayers of the Mass run in two columns: Latin on one side, the local language on the other. For a long time, Catholics of the Western church heard the Mass in Latin, whether they lived in Manila or Milwaukee, and followed along in books like this one. Then a pope, John the Twenty-Third, called the bishops of the world to Rome for a council. A story often told has him opening a window to show what he hoped it would do: let in fresh air.

The Second Vatican Council met in Rome over several autumns, and its documents changed ordinary church life. Take four of them. First, worship. The council allowed the Mass to be said in local languages, and asked that the people take a full, active part in it, not only watch. Soon parishes around the world heard the prayers in their own tongue. Some Catholics heard in this an echo of Pentecost in Acts, where, in the King James Bible, "every man heard them speak in his own language." Second, scripture. The council urged that the Bible be opened wide to ordinary Catholics, read, prayed and studied, not left to the clergy. Third, other Christians. The council spoke of Protestant and Orthodox Christians with new warmth, as brothers and sisters in Christ, still separated, and called Catholics to pray and work for unity. Fourth, other faiths. In a short document, the council said the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions. And it said plainly that the death of Christ cannot be charged against all the Jews of his time, or against Jews today, and it deplored hatred of Jews. Catholics still discuss how to read the council. Some see a long-overdue renewal. Some feel beauty and reverence were lost along the way, and some parishes still celebrate the older Latin Mass with permission. Both groups are reading the same documents. That's part of what a council leaves behind.
screen: `RESPECT FOR OTHER FAITHS, AND FOR JEWS.`

If you pray, pray in whatever words are truly yours.

964.title: Lifting the anathemas (1965)
964.hook: Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras lift the mutual excommunications from the old split between East and West
964.howItsDone: Delegations from Rome and from the patriarchate in Istanbul now visit each other on their churches' patronal feast days, and official dialogue between the two churches continues.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vatican II, and a pope who wanted fresh air. Your line: open the windows.

Two churches, one statement, read aloud on the same day in two cities. In Rome, at the end of the council, before the bishops. In Istanbul, the old Constantinople, in the patriarch's church. It's about something that happened long before anyone in either room was born. At the time of the great split between the Christian East and West, envoys from Rome and the patriarch in Constantinople had pronounced sentences of excommunication on each other. Those sentences sat on the record ever since, like a door slammed and never reopened. Now Pope Paul the Sixth and Patriarch Athenagoras agree to lift them.

An anathema is a solemn curse or ban, a sentence that puts someone outside the church. The word is in the New Testament. When Paul writes to the Galatians about anyone who preaches a different gospel, the King James Bible gives it as "let him be accursed." Strong words, meant for serious cases. The usual story of the old split: Envoys from Rome, in Constantinople, laid a document of excommunication on the altar of the great church there, and walked out. The patriarch and his synod answered with excommunications of their own. The quarrel had many roots, theology, authority, language, politics, and those sentences became a symbol of all of it. Then two men acted. Paul and Athenagoras had already met and embraced in Jerusalem. Now, in a joint declaration, they regretted the offensive words and hurtful actions of that time, and asked that the sentences be removed from memory and from the midst of the church, consigned to oblivion. What it didn't do matters too. It didn't restore full communion. The two churches still don't celebrate the Eucharist together, and their dialogue continues, patiently, on both sides. The declaration itself says the gesture isn't enough to end the differences. It was a start. Jesus put the order plainly, in the King James Bible: "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." The story goes that the old sentence from Rome was laid on an altar. The undoing began when both sides laid it aside.

Let one medium-sized old grudge come to mind: a cousin, an old friend, a former boss. Notice how long you've kept it on the record and what it costs to keep it there, and ask what lifting the sentence would mean, even if nothing else changes yet. If you pray, bring Jesus's words about leaving the gift at the altar.
anathema. Greek for a solemn curse, the old sentences of excommunication that Pope Paul the Sixth and Patriarch Athenagoras set aside between Rome and Constantinople.
Your line: nine hundred years undone. Undone, but not yet one. Day nine hundred sixty-four, complete.

965.title: Taizé
965.hook: Brother Roger's community in France welcomes young people from every church to sing and pray
965.howItsDone: Churches of different traditions hold Taizé-style evening prayers with short repeated chants, candles, scripture and silence, and young people travel to Taizé for a week of prayer and community life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the anathemas lifted, a pope and a patriarch setting down old sentences. Your line: nine hundred years undone.

Evening in a long, low church on a hill in the French countryside. No pews. Young people sit on the floor, on their knees, on little wooden stools, packed close. Candles. Orange cloth. A single short line is sung, and sung again, and again, until it's less a song than a kind of breathing. Then it changes language. Then, in the middle of the prayer, everything stops, and there's a long silence that nobody fills. Some of the people here are Catholic, some Protestant, some Orthodox, and some aren't sure what they are.

Roger Schutz was a young Swiss Protestant who came to the village of Taizé, in Burgundy, during the Second World War. He bought a house close to the line that divided France, and sheltered refugees there, among them Jews fleeing the Nazis. When the house was in danger, he had to leave. After the war he came back, and other men joined him. They became a community of brothers, living together under vows and praying together through the day, in time from Protestant backgrounds and from the Catholic Church, all living one life. Then young people started showing up, to pray, to talk, to work, and to sleep in tents and simple barracks. They kept coming, from many countries and churches. The brothers wrote songs anyone could join: a single line, often from scripture or an old prayer, repeated until it sinks in. One uses an old Latin hymn: "Ubi caritas et amor, Deus ibi est." Where charity and love are, God is there. The brothers don't try to start a new church or move anyone from theirs. They send people home, to their own parish, their own congregation. The prayer is meant to carry the joy of the gospel, a joy that doesn't depend on things going well. It sounds like the angel in Luke, in the King James Bible: "I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people." To all people. In a village in Burgundy, the door stays open to whoever comes.

Take one short line and repeat it slowly, sung, hummed or spoken: the old Latin, ubi caritas, where charity and love are, God is there, or the words of the thief beside Jesus on the cross, from Luke, which one Taizé chant sets to music: Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. Let it go round until you stop thinking about it, then let it fall away into silence.
Taizé. A village in France where Brother Roger's community of brothers from different churches welcomes young people to sing short chants and pray in silence.
Your line: the joy of the gospel. A joy that doesn't wait for things to go well. See you tomorrow.

966.title: Oscar Romero
966.hook: an archbishop in El Salvador speaks for the poor and is shot while saying Mass
966.howItsDone: The Catholic calendar marks Saint Oscar Romero's feast on the day of his death, and pilgrims visit the hospital chapel in San Salvador where he was killed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Taizé, one short line sung until it became breathing. Your line: the joy of the gospel.

A list of names, read aloud from the pulpit of the cathedral in San Salvador on a Sunday morning. First the archbishop has read the gospel and explained it. Now he reads the week's news. People taken from their homes. People found dead by the road. Priests, farmers, students. Across the country, in shops and farmhouses and city apartments, the radio carries his voice. For some families, it's the one place those names are said out loud. The archbishop is Oscar Romero, and when he was chosen, some expected him to keep quiet.

Romero was a careful, bookish priest when he was made archbishop, and some in power were glad of it. Soon after, his friend Rutilio Grande, a Jesuit who worked among poor farm families, was shot and killed on a country road, along with others traveling with him. Romero went to see the bodies. Those who knew him say something changed in him that night. He began to speak: for farmers whose land and lives were taken, for families of the disappeared, for the poor his country had pushed to the edge. He spoke against killing by any side. He used the pulpit and the radio, and when the church's radio station was bombed, he kept preaching. Proverbs, in the King James Bible: "Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction." Dumb there means unable to speak. People came to call Romero the voice of the voiceless. On his last Sunday he spoke straight to the soldiers. Paraphrased: you are our brothers, and no soldier has to obey an order to kill that goes against the law of God. He begged them, in God's name, to stop the repression. The next evening he was saying Mass in the hospital chapel where he lived, near cancer patients cared for by sisters. As he finished his sermon and turned toward the altar, a gunman fired through the open chapel door. He fell at the altar. The Catholic Church has since named him a saint, and Christians beyond it remember him too.
screen: `A FRIEND KILLED ON A COUNTRY ROAD.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose story doesn't get told: a worker nobody notices, a patient in a hallway, someone held somewhere, waiting. Hold one of them in mind and say their situation to yourself plainly, as if you were reading it on the radio. If you pray, pray for them, by name if you know it.
Oscar Romero. An archbishop of San Salvador who spoke for the poor and the disappeared, and was shot while saying Mass.

Your line: the voice of the voiceless. The week ran from a Birmingham cell to a hospital chapel, by way of a mountaintop, a little light, open windows, lifted sentences and Taizé. That's day nine hundred sixty-six.

chat.says: Why do people call Archbishop Romero the voice of the voiceless?
options: He used the pulpit and the radio to speak for the poor and the disappeared, whom others ignored.
He was a quiet, bookish man who spoke so softly that people struggled to hear him preach.
He ran a radio station that played music and news for people living far from a church.
chat.meaning: After Rutilio Grande's killing, Romero spoke for the poor and the families of the disappeared, from the pulpit and on the radio: open thy mouth for the dumb.
